prompt.context: Our client is a carpet manufacturing company, Benjamin Carpets. They produce a range of commercial and residential carpets which they sell through various distribution channels, mainly wholesalers although they do a small amount of direct sales to large accounts. They operate a single factory, 5 days a week with 2 8-hour shifts.
prompt.question: They are considering the purchase of a new piece of equipment, a yarn printer that will enable them to print colors and patterns directly onto carpet. They have asked you to assess whether this is a good decision. What do you think?

clarifying_info.q: What does the current manufacturing process look like?
clarifying_info.a: Current process: purchase pre-dyed yarn, load onto spools in production order, load onto weaver which weaves the carpet, attach backing, cut, roll, and store until shipment.

clarifying_info.q: What would the new process look like?
clarifying_info.a: New process: purchase undyed yarn, load onto spools and onto weaver; as this happens the printer prints color onto the carpet, then backing is attached, then cut, rolled, and stored until shipment.

clarifying_info.q: How much does the machine cost?
How much carpet do they produce per year?
clarifying_info.a: They produce 10M yards of carpet per year.

clarifying_info.q: What are the cost savings from the machine?
clarifying_info.a: Inventory savings of $0.50/yd (reduced yarn stock), labor savings of $0.25/yd (fewer changeovers), purchasing undyed yarn saves $0.50/yd, but the machine adds $1.00/yd in cost (dyes, maintenance, etc.). Net cost savings = $0.25/yd. Additional unquantified benefits: reduced obsolescence risk, increased just-in-time potential.

clarifying_info.q: What are the revenue opportunities from the machine?
clarifying_info.a: 1) Access to 5% of a 70M yard high-end carpet market. 2) 30% of current customers will trade up to higher-end product. They are not production constrained.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current selling price and cost per yard?
clarifying_info.a: They sell carpet now for $16/yard. Carpet costs $10/yard after cost savings.

clarifying_info.q: What is the high-end carpet selling price?
What is the cost of capital?

framework: Understand the machine and what it enables (manufacturing process change, new product capability)
Quantify cost savings: break down each savings/cost item and net them out across annual volume
Quantify revenue opportunities: new high-end market segment + existing customer upsell
Assess investment return: compare total annual benefit vs. cost of capital on $25M machine price
Consider qualitative factors: competitive necessity, plant feasibility, obsolescence risk, just-in-time upside
Recommendation: synthesize cost and revenue case into go/no-go with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: What is the net cost savings per yard from the machine, and what does that mean annually?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify all four cost line items and net them: +$0.50 (inventory) + $0.25 (labor) + $0.50 (undyed yarn) - $1.00 (dyes/maintenance) = $0.25/yd net savings. Applied to 10M yards/year = $2.5M/year. Candidate should also note unquantified benefits (obsolescence, JIT).

math.setup: Net savings per yard = inventory savings + labor savings + yarn cost savings - machine operating cost. Annual savings = net savings/yd x annual volume.
steps: At 10% cost of capital on $25M machine: required annual return = $25M x 10% = $2.5M/year
Cost savings alone = breakeven (and negative NPV if machine has finite life)
math.answer: Net cost savings of $0.25/yd; $2.5M/year total — exactly breakeven against the cost of capital, so cost savings alone do not justify the investment.

questions.prompt: What is the revenue upside from entering the high-end market (new customers)?
questions.guidance: Candidate must recognize that only the incremental contribution matters, not total revenue. New high-end market = 5% of 70M yards. Contribution = selling price minus current cost per yard (using $10 cost and $20 high-end price, but the marginal comparison is new revenue vs. what was previously earned). Strong candidates note: new customers generate contribution of $20 - $10 = $10/yd, but relative to selling standard carpet at $16 they generate an incremental uplift of $20 - $16 = $4/yd.

math.setup: New high-end volume = 5% x 70M yards. Incremental contribution = (high-end price - standard price) x new volume (since these are new customers not replacing existing).
steps: Annual contribution from new customers = $4/yd x 3.5M yd = $14M/year
Alternatively, full contribution = ($20 - $10) x 3.5M = $35M/year if treating as wholly new revenue
math.answer: $14M/year in incremental contribution (revenue uplift framing) or $35M/year (full contribution framing for new customers). The casebook uses the $35M figure.

questions.prompt: What is the revenue upside from existing customers trading up?
questions.guidance: 30% of existing 10M yards/year trade up from $16 standard to $20 high-end. The incremental contribution per yard is $20 - $16 = $4/yd. Candidate should recognize this is a contribution calculation, not a gross revenue calculation.

math.setup: Trade-up volume = 30% x 10M yd. Incremental contribution = (high-end price - standard price) x trade-up volume.
steps: Annual contribution from trade-up = $4/yd x 3M yd = $12M/year
math.answer: $12M/year in incremental contribution from existing customers trading up.

questions.prompt: Putting it all together: is this a good investment?
questions.guidance: Candidate should aggregate cost savings ($2.5M/year) + new customer contribution ($35M or $14M) + trade-up contribution ($12M) and compare to the capital cost hurdle ($2.5M/year at 10%). Strong candidates separate cost case (breakeven alone) from revenue case (very strong). The revenue case makes this a clearly compelling investment.

math.setup: Total annual benefit = cost savings + new customer contribution + trade-up contribution. Compare to cost-of-capital hurdle on $25M machine.
math.answer: Total incremental contribution of ~$47M/year from revenue growth alone far exceeds the $2.5M/year cost-of-capital hurdle on the $25M machine. This is a strong investment.

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the possible cost savings and revenue opportunities that should be considered when evaluating the yarn printer investment?

categories.name: Cost Savings
ideas: Inventory reduction ($0.50/yd) from holding less pre-dyed yarn SKUs
Labor savings ($0.25/yd) from reduced changeovers between color runs
Purchasing savings ($0.50/yd) from buying cheaper undyed yarn
Reduced obsolescence risk on pre-dyed yarn inventory
Increased just-in-time production potential (reduced finished goods inventory)
Possible overhead reduction if volume increases spread fixed costs

categories.name: Revenue Opportunities
ideas: Enter the high-end patterned/colored carpet market (5% share of 70M yd market)
Upsell existing customers to premium products (30% trade-up rate)
Custom/bespoke carpet designs for commercial accounts
Faster response to color trends (shorter lead times)
Reduced minimum order sizes enabling smaller accounts

categories.name: Risks and Costs
ideas: Machine operating costs: dyes, maintenance, etc. ($1.00/yd added cost)
Capital cost of $25M with finite machine life (negative NPV on cost savings alone)
Execution risk in changing manufacturing process
Dependency on new dye supply chain
Market risk: may not capture projected 5% of high-end market

recommendation: Recommend purchasing the yarn printer. The cost savings alone ($2.5M/year) barely justify the investment at 10% cost of capital, but the revenue opportunity is transformative: ~$47M/year in incremental contribution from entering the high-end market (3.5M yards at $4/yd uplift) and upselling existing customers (3M yards at $4/yd uplift).
The revenue case alone is more than 18x the annual cost-of-capital hurdle, making this a compelling investment even under conservative assumptions.
risks: Machine has finite life — cost savings alone produce negative NPV, so revenue projections must materialize
Achieving 5% of the high-end market and 30% customer trade-up are assumptions that require validation
$1.00/yd operating cost increase (dyes, maintenance) must be carefully managed
Process change carries execution and supply-chain risk
next_steps: Validate high-end market share assumption with sales team and market research
Model machine useful life and depreciation to confirm NPV is positive under various scenarios
Assess plant capacity to handle higher-value production mix
Identify and qualify undyed yarn suppliers
Plan change management and workforce training for new process
